prompt: What lets `sq(sq(gen(1, 2, 3)))` work with no new code?
hint: Compare the type `sq` takes with the type it returns.

choices.text: `sq` keeps a list of the numbers it has seen
choices.why: It keeps nothing; each value passes straight through.

choices.text: Its input and output are both `<-chan int`
choices.why: Right. A stage whose output type is its input type can be chained to itself.

choices.text: Go runs nested calls in parallel
choices.why: The calls themselves run in order; each starts a goroutine and returns at once.

choices.text: `gen` was written to be called twice
choices.why: `gen` was called once; it was `sq` that was used twice.

prompt: `overlap.go` passed five items through two stages of 20 ms each: 200 ms of work. At how many milliseconds did it finish?
hint: The last line of the output.

prompt: A pipeline has three stages taking 5 ms, 40 ms and 10 ms per item. A colleague makes the first stage twice as fast. What happens to the time for 1,000 items?
hint: What sets the pace of a pipeline?

choices.text: It halves
choices.why: Only the whole pipeline running twice as fast would halve it, and the first stage is not what sets the pace.

choices.text: It drops by about a third
choices.why: That would need the first stage to be a large share of the pace, and it is not the slowest.

choices.text: Barely changes: the 40 ms stage sets the pace
choices.why: Right. Items leave at the rate of the slowest stage; widen that one instead.

choices.text: It grows, because the fast stage floods the next one
choices.why: An unbuffered channel makes the fast stage wait; nothing floods.

prompt: In `overlap.go`, from 40 ms on, each line comes paired with another at the same instant. What does a pair show?
hint: Which items are the two lines about?

choices.text: Both stages busy at once
choices.why: Right: item n stored while item n+1 is read.

choices.text: One item being read twice
choices.why: Each pair names two different items.

choices.text: The channel holding two items
choices.why: The channel is unbuffered and holds nothing.

choices.text: The clock rounding two separate moments together
choices.why: Rounding to 10 ms could merge moments, but the steady pairing from 40 ms on is the overlap of the stages, which the 120 ms total confirms.

prompt: In a pipeline, which channel does each stage close?

choices.text: Its input, once it has read everything
choices.why: That would be a receiver closing a channel another goroutine sends on.

choices.text: The one it sends on
choices.why: Right, with `defer close(out)`, after its input has closed.

choices.text: Both, input and output
choices.why: Closing the input would panic the stage before it.

choices.text: None; `main` closes every channel at the end
choices.why: `main` does not even hold the middle channels.

prompt: `cascade.go` printed `gen: no more numbers, closing` before `main: 1`. What does that show?

choices.text: That `gen` closed too early and lost a number
choices.why: Both squares, 1 and 4, arrived.

choices.text: That `main` received from `gen` directly
choices.why: `main` ranges over `sq`'s output.

choices.text: Print order is not data order
choices.why: Right. `gen` had handed over its last number and closed while the squares were still in transit.

choices.text: That `defer` runs before the function's body
choices.why: A deferred call runs when the function returns.

prompt: `wide.go` runs its slow stage on three goroutines. Who closes that stage's output?

choices.text: Each of the three, with `defer close(out)`
choices.why: The second close would panic, and the first would hit the others' sends.

choices.text: The goroutine that finishes last, by checking `len(out)`
choices.why: `len` of an unbuffered channel says nothing about who is still sending.

choices.text: `gen`, when it runs out of numbers
choices.why: `gen` closes only its own output.

choices.text: A goroutine that waits on a `WaitGroup`
choices.why: Right: lesson 14's closer, because only a count knows the last sender.

prompt: In `wide.go`, six items of 30 ms took 180 ms at width 1. How many milliseconds did they take at width 3?
hint: The second line of the output.

prompt: `stuck.go` read two results and printed `goroutines still alive: 3`. Which goroutines were they?
hint: Count the stages, and the one reading.

choices.text: Three copies of `sq`
choices.why: `stuck.go` called `sq` once.

choices.text: `main`, `gen` and `sq`
choices.why: Right: the two stages are blocked on sends nobody will receive.

choices.text: `main`, the garbage collector and the timer
choices.why: `runtime.NumGoroutine` here counts the program's own goroutines, and two of them are the stages.

choices.text: Three stages waiting for `main` to close them
choices.why: There are two stages, and they are waiting to send.

prompt: Why can the close cascade of section 03 not free the stages in `stuck.go`?

choices.text: `main` does not call `close` on `results`
choices.why: A reader closing a channel others send on would panic them; that is not the way out.

choices.text: Closing travels downstream; they are upstream
choices.why: Right. Only a signal travelling upstream, a context, can reach them.

choices.text: `defer close(out)` runs when `main` exits
choices.why: It runs when the stage's own goroutine returns, which never happens here.

choices.text: The thousand numbers have not all been generated
choices.why: True, and the reason is that `gen` is blocked, which is the problem itself.

prompt: In `stoppable.go`, `main` waits with `stages.Wait()` before counting goroutines. What would counting straight after `cancel()` risk?

choices.text: Nothing; `cancel` returns after the stages have stopped
choices.why: `cancel` closes the `Done` channel and returns; the stages stop afterwards, in their own time.

choices.text: A number taken too soon, still showing 3
choices.why: Right. Cancelling asks; the `WaitGroup` is what knows the stages have finished.

choices.text: A panic from counting a cancelled goroutine
choices.why: Counting never panics, and goroutines are not themselves cancelled.

choices.text: A race report on `runtime.NumGoroutine`
choices.why: It is safe to call at any time; the risk is a wrong number, not a race.

prompt: In a stoppable stage, every send sits inside a `select` with a second case, `case <-ctx.___():`.
hint: The method returning the channel a context closes when it ends.

prompt: Put the shutdown of `stoppable.go` in order, from the moment `main` has its two results.
Match each pipeline habit with the failure it prevents.
hint: Three habits, three failures from lessons 6 and 14.

pairs.left: closing only the channel you send on
pairs.right: a send on a closed channel
stages stuck after the reader left

prompt: Which of these does a stage of `stoppable.go` do? Choose all that apply.
hint: The last paragraph of section 04 lists the full pattern.

choices.text: Receives its input with `range`
choices.why: Yes, so its input's close ends its loop.

choices.text: Sends inside a `select` on `ctx.Done()`
choices.why: Yes, so a cancel can reach it while it waits.

choices.text: Closes its input when cancelled
choices.why: It closes only its output; its input belongs to the stage before.

choices.text: Calls `cancel` when it runs out of work
choices.why: Running out of work is signalled by closing, not cancelling; only `main` cancels.

prompt: A server builds `stuck.go`'s pipeline for every request and reads two results. After 10,000 requests, roughly how many stage goroutines are left blocked?
hint: Each request leaves its two stages behind.

choices.text: None, because each request's goroutines end with the request
choices.why: Nothing ends a goroutine but returning, and these never return.

choices.text: Two, since the stages are shared
choices.why: Each request built its own pipeline, with its own stages.

choices.text: 10,000, one per request
choices.why: There are two stages per pipeline.
Right: two per request, for ever, the leak of lesson 6.
